claim: At trunk levels of the avian axis, neural crest progenitors sequentially emigrate from the neural tube for a period of about two days.
source: At trunk levels of the avian axis, NC progenitors sequentially emigrate from the NT for a period of about two days while actively proliferating before and after delamination and largely synchronizing to the S-phase of the cell cycle during the emigration event (Burstyn-Cohen and Kalcheim, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Burstyn-Cohen and Kalcheim, 2002).

claim: Neural crest progenitors actively proliferate before and after delamination.
source: At trunk levels of the avian axis, NC progenitors sequentially emigrate from the NT for a period of about two days while actively proliferating before and after delamination and largely synchronizing to the S-phase of the cell cycle during the emigration event (Burstyn-Cohen and Kalcheim, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Burstyn-Cohen and Kalcheim, 2002).

claim: Neural crest progenitors largely synchronize to the S-phase of the cell cycle during the emigration event.
source: At trunk levels of the avian axis, NC progenitors sequentially emigrate from the NT for a period of about two days while actively proliferating before and after delamination and largely synchronizing to the S-phase of the cell cycle during the emigration event (Burstyn-Cohen and Kalcheim, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Burstyn-Cohen and Kalcheim, 2002).

claim: Roof plate progenitors originate ventral to the cohort of premigratory neural crest.
source: Lineage-tracing experiments showed that RP progenitors originate ventral to the cohort of premigratory NC (Krispin et al., 2010b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to lineage-tracing experiments (Krispin et al., 2010b).

claim: As a result of continuous cell emigration, roof plate precursors undergo a ventro-dorsal shift.
source: As a result of continuous cell emigration, RP precursors undergo a ventro-dorsal shift and, upon completion of NC departure, they reach the dorsal midline of the NT and form the definitive RP (Krispin et al., 2010b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Krispin et al., 2010b).

claim: Upon completion of neural crest departure, roof plate precursors reach the dorsal midline of the neural tube and form the definitive roof plate.
source: As a result of continuous cell emigration, RP precursors undergo a ventro-dorsal shift and, upon completion of NC departure, they reach the dorsal midline of the NT and form the definitive RP (Krispin et al., 2010b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Krispin et al., 2010b).

claim: Roof plate progenitors gradually exit the cell cycle to become post-mitotic.
source: RP progenitors gradually exit the cell cycle to become post-mitotic (Kahane and Kalcheim, 1998), and function primarily as a dorsal organizer, providing a gradient of Bone Morphogenetic Protein (BMP) and Wnt activity which is crucial for development of dorsal interneurons (Chizhikov and Millen, 2005; Le Dréau and Martí, 2013; Muroyama et al., 2002; Zechner et al., 2007) and for proliferation of ependymal cells at later stages (Shinozuka et al., 2019; Xing et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Kahane and Kalcheim, 1998).

claim: The roof plate functions primarily as a dorsal organizer, providing a gradient of Bone Morphogenetic Protein (BMP) and Wnt activity.
source: RP progenitors gradually exit the cell cycle to become post-mitotic (Kahane and Kalcheim, 1998), and function primarily as a dorsal organizer, providing a gradient of Bone Morphogenetic Protein (BMP) and Wnt activity which is crucial for development of dorsal interneurons (Chizhikov and Millen, 2005; Le Dréau and Martí, 2013; Muroyama et al., 2002; Zechner et al., 2007) and for proliferation of ependymal cells at later stages (Shinozuka et al., 2019; Xing et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Chizhikov and Millen, 2005; Le Dréau and Martí, 2013; Muroyama et al., 2002; Zechner et al., 2007).

claim: The gradient of BMP and Wnt activity from the roof plate is crucial for development of dorsal interneurons.
source: RP progenitors gradually exit the cell cycle to become post-mitotic (Kahane and Kalcheim, 1998), and function primarily as a dorsal organizer, providing a gradient of Bone Morphogenetic Protein (BMP) and Wnt activity which is crucial for development of dorsal interneurons (Chizhikov and Millen, 2005; Le Dréau and Martí, 2013; Muroyama et al., 2002; Zechner et al., 2007) and for proliferation of ependymal cells at later stages (Shinozuka et al., 2019; Xing et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Chizhikov and Millen, 2005; Le Dréau and Martí, 2013; Muroyama et al., 2002; Zechner et al., 2007).

claim: The gradient of BMP and Wnt activity from the roof plate is crucial for proliferation of ependymal cells at later stages.
source: RP progenitors gradually exit the cell cycle to become post-mitotic (Kahane and Kalcheim, 1998), and function primarily as a dorsal organizer, providing a gradient of Bone Morphogenetic Protein (BMP) and Wnt activity which is crucial for development of dorsal interneurons (Chizhikov and Millen, 2005; Le Dréau and Martí, 2013; Muroyama et al., 2002; Zechner et al., 2007) and for proliferation of ependymal cells at later stages (Shinozuka et al., 2019; Xing et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Shinozuka et al., 2019; Xing et al., 2018).

claim: BMP derived from the non-neural ectoderm participates in neural crest induction at the neural plate border in the early neurula.
source: In the early neurula, BMP is derived from the non-neural ectoderm and participates in NC induction at the neural plate border (Endo et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Endo et al., 2002).

claim: Upon closure of the neural tube, cells of the dorsal domain synthesize and secrete BMP.
source: Upon closure of the NT, cells of the dorsal domain synthesize and secrete BMP, which acts in a graded rostro-caudal fashion to activate Wnt signaling and a network of downstream genes that altogether promote NC EMT and emigration (Reviewed in Kalcheim, 2018; Theveneau and Mayor, 2012a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to review articles (Kalcheim, 2018; Theveneau and Mayor, 2012a).

claim: BMP acts in a graded rostro-caudal fashion to activate Wnt signaling and a network of downstream genes that promote neural crest EMT and emigration.
source: Upon closure of the NT, cells of the dorsal domain synthesize and secrete BMP, which acts in a graded rostro-caudal fashion to activate Wnt signaling and a network of downstream genes that altogether promote NC EMT and emigration (Reviewed in Kalcheim, 2018; Theveneau and Mayor, 2012a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to review articles (Kalcheim, 2018; Theveneau and Mayor, 2012a).

claim: Approaching the end of neural crest production in the avian embryo, the dorsal neural tube becomes insensitive to BMP.
source: A first step toward understanding the segregation between NC and RP, was the finding that approaching the end of the NC production in the avian embryo, the dorsal NT becomes insensitive to BMP, even though this factor continues to be produced by nascent RP cells.
evidence: This claim is stated as a finding from previous work.

claim: BMP continues to be produced by nascent roof plate cells even when the dorsal neural tube becomes insensitive to it.
source: A first step toward understanding the segregation between NC and RP, was the finding that approaching the end of the NC production in the avian embryo, the dorsal NT becomes insensitive to BMP, even though this factor continues to be produced by nascent RP cells.
evidence: This claim is stated as a finding from previous work.

claim: Local downregulation of BMP signaling is necessary for the end of neural crest stage.
source: This suggested that local downregulation of BMP signaling is necessary for the end of NC stage, a conclusion further illustrated by a premature cessation of NC proliferation and delamination upon early inhibition of BMP signaling (Nitzan et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Nitzan et al., 2016).

claim: Early inhibition of BMP signaling causes premature cessation of neural crest proliferation and delamination.
source: This suggested that local downregulation of BMP signaling is necessary for the end of NC stage, a conclusion further illustrated by a premature cessation of NC proliferation and delamination upon early inhibition of BMP signaling (Nitzan et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Nitzan et al., 2016).

claim: The transcription factor HES1/Hairy1 mediates BMP-dependent events in neural crest development.
source: These events were mediated by the transcription factor HES1/Hairy1, as early misexpression of hes1/hairy1 in the dorsal NT led to a downregulation of the Alk3 BMP receptor and of pSmad activity (Nitzan et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Nitzan et al., 2016).

claim: Early misexpression of hes1/hairy1 in the dorsal neural tube leads to downregulation of the Alk3 BMP receptor.
source: These events were mediated by the transcription factor HES1/Hairy1, as early misexpression of hes1/hairy1 in the dorsal NT led to a downregulation of the Alk3 BMP receptor and of pSmad activity (Nitzan et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Nitzan et al., 2016).

claim: Early misexpression of hes1/hairy1 in the dorsal neural tube leads to downregulation of pSmad activity.
source: These events were mediated by the transcription factor HES1/Hairy1, as early misexpression of hes1/hairy1 in the dorsal NT led to a downregulation of the Alk3 BMP receptor and of pSmad activity (Nitzan et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Nitzan et al., 2016).

claim: A recent RNA-seq analysis revealed transcriptional heterogeneity between premigratory neural crest and definitive roof plate cells.
source: A recent RNA-seq analysis revealed transcriptional heterogeneity between premigratory NC and definitive RP cells, uncovering a set of genes expressed specifically at the onset of the RP stage (Ofek et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Ofek et al., 2021).

claim: Raldh2/Aldh1a2 is one of the genes expressed specifically at the onset of the roof plate stage.
source: A recent RNA-seq analysis revealed transcriptional heterogeneity between premigratory NC and definitive RP cells, uncovering a set of genes expressed specifically at the onset of the RP stage (Ofek et al., 2021). One of these genes is Raldh2/Aldh1a2, that encodes an enzyme responsible for the biosynthesis of the morphogen retinoic acid (RA) (Haselbeck et al., 1999), central to multiple neurodevelopmental processes (Diez del Corral and Morales, 2014; Lara-Ramírez et al., 2013; Wilson et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Ofek et al., 2021; Haselbeck et al., 1999).

claim: Raldh2/Aldh1a2 encodes an enzyme responsible for the biosynthesis of retinoic acid.
source: One of these genes is Raldh2/Aldh1a2, that encodes an enzyme responsible for the biosynthesis of the morphogen retinoic acid (RA) (Haselbeck et al., 1999), central to multiple neurodevelopmental processes (Diez del Corral and Morales, 2014; Lara-Ramírez et al., 2013; Wilson et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Haselbeck et al., 1999).

claim: Retinoic acid is central to multiple neurodevelopmental processes.
source: One of these genes is Raldh2/Aldh1a2, that encodes an enzyme responsible for the biosynthesis of the morphogen retinoic acid (RA) (Haselbeck et al., 1999), central to multiple neurodevelopmental processes (Diez del Corral and Morales, 2014; Lara-Ramírez et al., 2013; Wilson et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Diez del Corral and Morales, 2014; Lara-Ramírez et al., 2013; Wilson et al., 2004).

claim: Retinoic acid derived from the Raldh2-expressing somitic mesoderm is a key factor in neural tube development.
source: RA derived from the Raldh2-expressing somitic mesoderm has been described as a key factor in NT development, including control of motoneuron specification (Novitch et al., 2003; Wilson et al., 2004) and initiation but not maintenance of NC EMT and emigration (Martínez-Morales et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Novitch et al., 2003; Wilson et al., 2004; Martínez-Morales et al., 2011).

claim: Retinoic acid from the somitic mesoderm controls motoneuron specification.
source: RA derived from the Raldh2-expressing somitic mesoderm has been described as a key factor in NT development, including control of motoneuron specification (Novitch et al., 2003; Wilson et al., 2004) and initiation but not maintenance of NC EMT and emigration (Martínez-Morales et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Novitch et al., 2003; Wilson et al., 2004).

claim: Retinoic acid from the somitic mesoderm initiates but does not maintain neural crest EMT and emigration.
source: RA derived from the Raldh2-expressing somitic mesoderm has been described as a key factor in NT development, including control of motoneuron specification (Novitch et al., 2003; Wilson et al., 2004) and initiation but not maintenance of NC EMT and emigration (Martínez-Morales et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Martínez-Morales et al., 2011).

claim: Expression of Raldh2 in the dorsal neural tube was previously reported.
source: Although expression of Raldh2 in the dorsal NT was previously reported (Berggren et al., 1999; Blentic et al., 2003), its precise temporal dynamics vis-à-vis NC/RP phases and function/s have not been characterized.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Berggren et al., 1999; Blentic et al., 2003).

claim: At an early neural crest stage, Raldh2 is expressed in the intermediate and paraxial somitic mesoderm but not in the neuroepithelium.
source: At an early NC stage, Raldh2 was expressed in the intermediate and paraxial somitic mesoderm but not in the neuroepithelium (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: At an advanced neural crest stage, Raldh2 continues to be transcribed in subdomains of the somite-derived sclerotome and dermomyotome.
source: At an advanced NC stage, Raldh2 continued to be transcribed in subdomains of the somite-derived sclerotome and dermomyotome (Figure 1C) and was weakly detected in the dorsal NT (Figure 1C, arrowhead).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: At an advanced neural crest stage, Raldh2 is weakly detected in the dorsal neural tube.
source: At an advanced NC stage, Raldh2 continued to be transcribed in subdomains of the somite-derived sclerotome and dermomyotome (Figure 1C) and was weakly detected in the dorsal NT (Figure 1C, arrowhead).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Raldh2 is strongly expressed in the nascent roof plate.
source: Subsequently, Raldh2 was strongly expressed in the nascent RP itself (Figure 1D, arrowhead, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: No expression of Cyp1B1 is apparent in the neural tube at any stage examined.
source: In contrast, no expression of Cyp1B1 was apparent in the NT at any stage, although robust transcription was evident in the paraxial mesoderm throughout development (Figure 1E–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1E–G.

claim: Robust transcription of Cyp1B1 is evident in the paraxial mesoderm throughout development.
source: In contrast, no expression of Cyp1B1 was apparent in the NT at any stage, although robust transcription was evident in the paraxial mesoderm throughout development (Figure 1E–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1E–G.

claim: At the early neural crest stage, Cyp26A1 is absent from the neural tube and adjacent mesoderm.
source: At an early NC stage, Cyp26A1 was absent from the NT and adjacent mesoderm, it was later detected in a salt and pepper pattern in dorsal interneuron progenitors, but was excluded from the dorsal midline (Figure 1H–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1H–I.

claim: Cyp26A1 is later detected in a salt and pepper pattern in dorsal interneuron progenitors but is excluded from the dorsal midline.
source: At an early NC stage, Cyp26A1 was absent from the NT and adjacent mesoderm, it was later detected in a salt and pepper pattern in dorsal interneuron progenitors, but was excluded from the dorsal midline (Figure 1H–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1H–I.

claim: As the definitive roof plate forms, Cyp26A1 is occasionally detected in roof plate cells.
source: As the definitive RP formed, it was also occasionally detected in RP cells (Figure 1J).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: At the early neural crest stage, there is no prominent expression of CRABP1 in either the neural tube or paraxial mesoderm.
source: At the early NC stage, there was no prominent expression of CRABP1 in either the NT or paraxial mesoderm (Figure 1K); at an advanced NC stage it appeared in the basal domain of the NT, corresponding to the positions adopted by differentiating neurons, yet absent from the dorsal and ventral midline regions (Figure 1L).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1K.

claim: At an advanced neural crest stage, CRABP1 appears in the basal domain of the neural tube, corresponding to the positions adopted by differentiating neurons, yet is absent from the dorsal and ventral midline regions.
source: At the early NC stage, there was no prominent expression of CRABP1 in either the NT or paraxial mesoderm (Figure 1K); at an advanced NC stage it appeared in the basal domain of the NT, corresponding to the positions adopted by differentiating neurons, yet absent from the dorsal and ventral midline regions (Figure 1L).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1L.

claim: At the roof plate stage, CRABP1 is additionally expressed in two stripes at the lateral domain of the roof plate.
source: At the RP stage, CRABP1 was additionally expressed in two stripes at the lateral domain of the RP (Figure 1M, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, and see Ofek et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1M and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, and is consistent with previous work (Ofek et al., 2021).

claim: RARα, RARβ and RXRγ are expressed in the dorsal neural tube at the nascent roof plate stage.
source: Expression of all RA receptors was predominantly ubiquitous in both early NC (Diez del Corral et al., 2003) and RP stages with at least one variant of each subunit expressed in the dorsal NT at the nascent RP stage (RARα, RARβ and RXRγ, but not RARγ or RXRα) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and is consistent with previous work (Diez del Corral et al., 2003).

claim: RARγ and RXRα are not expressed in the dorsal neural tube at the nascent roof plate stage.
source: Expression of all RA receptors was predominantly ubiquitous in both early NC (Diez del Corral et al., 2003) and RP stages with at least one variant of each subunit expressed in the dorsal NT at the nascent RP stage (RARα, RARβ and RXRγ, but not RARγ or RXRα) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: RARE activity is primarily present within the dorsal half of the neural tube at both neural crest and roof plate stages.
source: Whereas control RFP was apparent throughout the dorso-ventral extent of the NTs, RARE activity was primarily present within the dorsal half of the NT at both stages (Figure 1N–O').
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using a RARE reporter shown in Figure 1N–O'.

claim: During the transition from neural crest to definitive roof plate, the latter becomes a local source of retinoic acid.
source: Together, these data show that whereas NC cells respond to mesoderm-derived RA (see Introduction for refs.), but do not synthesize it, the emerging RP both synthesizes and responds to this factor. Hence during the transition from NC to definitive RP, the latter becomes a local source of RA.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined data on Raldh2 expression and RARE activity.

claim: BMP signaling is essential for neural crest EMT and emigration.
source: In previous studies, we showed that BMP signaling is essential for NC EMT and emigration (Sela-Donenfeld and Kalcheim, 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Sela-Donenfeld and Kalcheim, 1999).

claim: When approaching the roof plate stage, although BMP is still produced by the nascent roof plate, the latter becomes refractory to it.
source: Subsequently, when approaching the RP stage, although BMP is still produced by the nascent RP, the latter becomes refractory to it, likely via downregulation of BMP receptor 1 A (Alk3), and upregulation of BMP inhibitory genes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B; Nitzan et al., 2016; Ofek et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Nitzan et al., 2016; Ofek et al., 2021) and RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The nascent roof plate becomes refractory to BMP likely via downregulation of BMP receptor 1 A (Alk3).
source: Subsequently, when approaching the RP stage, although BMP is still produced by the nascent RP, the latter becomes refractory to it, likely via downregulation of BMP receptor 1 A (Alk3), and upregulation of BMP inhibitory genes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B; Nitzan et al., 2016; Ofek et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Nitzan et al., 2016; Ofek et al., 2021) and RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The nascent roof plate becomes refractory to BMP via upregulation of BMP inhibitory genes.
source: Subsequently, when approaching the RP stage, although BMP is still produced by the nascent RP, the latter becomes refractory to it, likely via downregulation of BMP receptor 1 A (Alk3), and upregulation of BMP inhibitory genes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B; Nitzan et al., 2016; Ofek et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Nitzan et al., 2016; Ofek et al., 2021) and RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: RARα403 and Cyp26A1 can be effectively used to inhibit RA signaling.
source: First, the efficacy of these constructs was tested by co-electroporation with RARE-RFP. RFP intensity was significantly reduced by 79% and 88% in Cyp26A1- and RARα403-electroporated embryos, respectively, when compared to GFP-only controls. Similarly, RARα403 almost completely abolished the RARE-AP signal observed in controls (Figure 2—figure supplement 1). Thus, both RARα403 and Cyp26A1 can be effectively used to examine the consequences of RA signaling inhibition.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: RFP intensity from RARE-RFP is significantly reduced by 79% in Cyp26A1-electroporated embryos compared to GFP-only controls.
source: First, the efficacy of these constructs was tested by co-electroporation with RARE-RFP. RFP intensity was significantly reduced by 79% and 88% in Cyp26A1- and RARα403-electroporated embryos, respectively, when compared to GFP-only controls.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: RFP intensity from RARE-RFP is significantly reduced by 88% in RARα403-electroporated embryos compared to GFP-only controls.
source: First, the efficacy of these constructs was tested by co-electroporation with RARE-RFP. RFP intensity was significantly reduced by 79% and 88% in Cyp26A1- and RARα403-electroporated embryos, respectively, when compared to GFP-only controls.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: RARα403 almost completely abolishes the RARE-AP signal observed in controls.
source: Similarly, RARα403 almost completely abolished the RARE-AP signal observed in controls (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: pSmad is strongly expressed in the dorsal neural tube at the neural crest stage.
source: First, we monitored pSmad 1/5/9 expression, a readout of BMP activity, at the NC stage. Control GFP was delivered to embryos aged 27 somite pairs followed by fixation 12 hr later. pSmad was strongly expressed in the dorsal NT (Figure 2A and A'), corroborating previous findings (Nitzan et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2A and A', and is consistent with previous work (Nitzan et al., 2016).

claim: The roof plate of control embryos is devoid of BMP activity at the roof plate stage.
source: As expected (Nitzan et al., 2016), the RP of control embryos was already devoid of BMP activity at this stage (Figure 2B and B', arrows).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2B and B', and is consistent with previous work (Nitzan et al., 2016).

claim: The roof plate domain of embryos treated with either RARα403 or Cyp26A1 is pSmad-positive, indicating a failure to normally downregulate BMP signaling.
source: In contrast, the RP domain of embryos treated with either RARα403 or Cyp26A1 was pSmad-positive, indicating a failure to normally downregulate BMP signaling (Figure 2C–D', arrowheads).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2C–D'.

claim: Quantification of pSmad intensity confirms a significant increase in Cyp26A1 and RARα403-treated embryos compared to controls.
source: Quantification of pSmad intensity confirmed a significant increase in Cyp26A1 and RARα403-treated embryos compared to controls. This was apparent even if measurement of pSmad intensity comprised the dorsal NT from its midline to the ventral border of pSmad+ staining, that included dI1 progenitors (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Inhibition of RA signaling extends BMP activity into the roof plate stage by preventing its normal downregulation during the transition from neural crest to roof plate.
source: These results show that inhibition of RA signaling extends BMP activity into the RP stage by preventing its normal downregulation during the transition from NC to RP.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data on pSmad expression.

claim: Embryos electroporated with either Cyp26A1 or RARα403 exhibit a substantially decreased intensity of BAMBI mRNA staining in the roof plate relative to controls.
source: Embryos electroporated with either Cyp26A1 or RARα403 at E2.5 exhibited a substantially decreased intensity of BAMBI mRNA staining in the RP relative to controls (Figure 2F–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2F–I.

claim: RARα403 significantly affects the upregulation of hairy1 in roof plate when compared to control embryos.
source: Similarly, RARα403 significantly affected the upregulation of both hairy1 and Grem1 in RP when compared to control embryos (Figure 2J–O).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2J–O.

claim: RARα403 significantly affects the upregulation of Grem1 in roof plate when compared to control embryos.
source: Similarly, RARα403 significantly affected the upregulation of both hairy1 and Grem1 in RP when compared to control embryos (Figure 2J–O).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2J–O.

claim: The downregulation of BMP signaling by RA is accounted for, at least partially, by upregulation of BMP inhibitory genes.
source: These results show that the downregulation of BMP signaling by RA is accounted for, at least partially, by upregulation of BMP inhibitory genes.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data on BMP inhibitor expression.

claim: Significant activity of the Wnt pathway is observed in the early dorsal neural tube and emigrating neural crest cells.
source: Whereas significant activity of the Wnt pathway was observed in the early dorsal NT and emigrating NC cells, a substantial decrease in 12XTopFlashd2GFP expression was apparent in the normal RP (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A-B', D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using a Wnt reporter shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A-B', D.

claim: A substantial decrease in 12XTopFlashd2GFP expression is apparent in the normal roof plate.
source: Whereas significant activity of the Wnt pathway was observed in the early dorsal NT and emigrating NC cells, a substantial decrease in 12XTopFlashd2GFP expression was apparent in the normal RP (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A-B', D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using a Wnt reporter shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A-B', D.

claim: A significantly enhanced expression of 12XTopFlashd2GFP is measured in the roof plate of RARα403-transfected neural tubes.
source: In contrast, a significantly enhanced expression was measured in the RP of RARα403-transfected NTs (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C-D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using a Wnt reporter shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C-D.

claim: Inhibition of RA signaling extends Wnt activity into the roof plate stage by preventing its normal downregulation during the transition from neural crest to roof plate.
source: These results show that inhibition of RA signaling extends Wnt activity into the RP stage by preventing its normal downregulation during the transition from NC to RP.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data on Wnt reporter expression.

claim: RA is necessary for the downregulation of BMP and of downstream Wnt signaling towards ending neural crest production and/or emigration.
source: Hence, RA is necessary for the downregulation of BMP and of downstream Wnt signaling towards ending NC production and/or emigration.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined experimental data on BMP and Wnt signaling.

claim: Foxd3, snai2, and sox9 are known premigratory markers of trunk neural crest cells.
source: Foxd3, snai2, and sox9 are known premigratory markers of trunk NC cells (Nieto et al., 1994; Sela-Donenfeld and Kalcheim, 1999), and are downregulated in the dorsal NT upon emigration of neural progenitors, being absent from prospective melanoblasts and RP (Krispin et al., 2010b; Nitzan et al., 2013; Ofek et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Nieto et al., 1994; Sela-Donenfeld and Kalcheim, 1999).

claim: Foxd3, snai2, and sox9 are downregulated in the dorsal neural tube upon emigration of neural progenitors, being absent from prospective melanoblasts and roof plate.
source: Foxd3, snai2, and sox9 are known premigratory markers of trunk NC cells (Nieto et al., 1994; Sela-Donenfeld and Kalcheim, 1999), and are downregulated in the dorsal NT upon emigration of neural progenitors, being absent from prospective melanoblasts and RP (Krispin et al., 2010b; Nitzan et al., 2013; Ofek et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Krispin et al., 2010b; Nitzan et al., 2013; Ofek et al., 2021).

claim: In the absence of RA activity, foxd3, snai2, and sox9 transcripts persist in the dorsal neural tube at the roof plate stage.
source: Expression of foxd3, snai2, and sox9 transcripts was examined at the RP stage in embryos electroporated with RARα403. Strikingly, whereas no mRNA expression was detected in controls, all three genes persisted in the dorsal NT of treated embryos (Figure 3A–F', arrowheads).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3A–F'.

claim: Sox9 protein is maintained in the dorsal neural tube at the roof plate stage in both Cyp26A1- and RARα403-electroporated embryos.
source: Moreover, using immunohistochemistry to assess Sox9 protein, we confirmed its maintenance in the dorsal NT at the RP stage both in Cyp26A1- and RARα403-electroporated embryos (Figure 3G–J).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3G–J.

claim: Endogenous RA signaling underlies the loss of neural crest identity towards the end of the neural crest period.
source: These findings suggest that endogenous RA signaling underlies the loss of NC identity towards the end of the NC period.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data on neural crest marker expression.

claim: A significantly higher number of mitotic nuclei is observed in the roof plate of embryos treated with either Cyp26A1 or RARα403 compared to controls.
source: Remarkably, a significantly higher number of mitotic nuclei was observed in the RP of embryos treated with either Cyp26A1 or RARα403 compared to controls which exhibited a low extent of mitosis (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data for phospho-Histone H3 shown in Figure 4A–D.

claim: Endogenous RA inhibits cell proliferation in the dorsal neural tube.
source: These results suggest that endogenous RA inhibits cell proliferation, consistent with previous data obtained in forebrain and optic tectum of avian embryos (Gupta and Sen, 2015; Kukreja et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data on cell proliferation and is consistent with previous work (Gupta and Sen, 2015; Kukreja et al., 2020).

claim: In control embryos at the roof plate stage, most nuclei are restricted to the basal domain of the roof plate.
source: Characteristic of post-mitotic, differentiating progenitors is the localization of nuclei to the basal domain of the neuroepithelium, as observed in control embryos at the RP stage (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: In RARα403-electroporated embryos, nuclei are spread throughout the apico-basal extent of the roof plate.
source: In contrast, in RARα403-electroporated embryos, nuclei were spread throughout its apico-basal extent. Quantification showed that their localization to the apical half of the epithelium significantly exceeds that seen in control conditions (Figure 4E–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 4E–G.

claim: The normal roof plate has a continuous and prominent laminin-containing basal lamina.
source: One of these traits is the deposition of a continuous and prominent laminin-containing basal lamina covering the normal RP (Figure 4H and H').
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4H and H'.

claim: Inhibition of RA signaling results in a weaker and discontinuous pattern of laminin immunostaining dorsal to the roof plate.
source: Inhibition of RA signaling resulted in a weaker and discontinuous pattern of laminin immunostaining dorsal to the RP (Figure 4I–J), indicative of the maintenance of NC characteristics at the later RP stage.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4I–J.

claim: In the absence of RA activity, many cells are devoid of epithelial integrity, including labeled cells detaching from the epithelium.
source: Consistently, upon electroporation with membrane-tethered GFP, it was apparent in controls that cells extended along the apico-basal domain of the RP (Figure 4H). In contrast, in the absence of RA activity, many cells were devoid of epithelial integrity, including labeled cells detaching from the epithelium (Figure 4I, arrows).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Inhibition of RA signaling in the dorsal neural tube prevents cells from exiting the cell cycle and from adopting cellular traits that characterize the normal ontogeny of a roof plate.
source: Combined, these results show that inhibition of RA signaling in the dorsal NT prevents cells from exiting the cell cycle and from adopting cellular traits that characterize the normal ontogeny of a RP.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined experimental data on cell proliferation and epithelial traits.

claim: The number of emigrated, late GFP-labeled cells is significantly higher on the RARα403-electroporated side when compared to the control contralateral side and also to both sides of control embryos.
source: However, the number of emigrated, late GFP-labeled cells was significantly higher on the RARα403-electroporated side when compared to the control contralateral side and also to both sides of control embryos (Figure 5B–D, arrowheads in C').
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B–D.

claim: RA signaling promotes the end of neural crest cell delamination.
source: These data show that RA signaling promotes the end of NC cell delamination.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data on late emigration.

claim: Co-transfection of Smad6 and RARα403 inhibits the RARα403-dependent extension of cellular EMT.
source: Co-transfection of Smad6 and RARα403 inhibited the RARα403-dependent extension of cellular EMT (Figure 5H–H'1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5H–H'1.

claim: Late RA signaling ends the period of cell emigration in a BMP-dependent manner.
source: Together, these results suggest that late RA signaling ends the period of cell emigration in a BMP-dependent manner.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data on the interaction between RA and BMP signaling in regulating emigration.

claim: 95% ± 0.8% of the late-delaminating GFP-labeled cells are HNK1+.
source: Remarkably, 95% ± 0.8% of the late-delaminating GFP-labeled cells were HNK1+ (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), confirming their NC nature.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: In RARα403-treated embryos, foxd3 expression is evident in the dorsal neural tube and also in neural crest cells that presumably emigrated recently.
source: In RARα403-treated embryos foxd3 expression was evident in the dorsal NT (see also Figure 3), and also in NC cells that presumably emigrated recently (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D-E', arrowheads), further confirming their NC identity.
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D-E'.

claim: Local RA inhibition in the neural tube extends the period of neural crest production and further delamination into the roof plate stage.
source: Thus, local RA inhibition in the NT extends the period of NC production and further delamination into the RP stage.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined experimental data on late emigration and neural crest marker expression.

claim: RA is a major regulator of the end of the neural crest stage.
source: Collectively, these results point to RA being a major regulator of the end of the NC stage.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined experimental data.

claim: The number of sections or segments with pSmad, Sox9, or foxd3 expression does not differ between control and VP16-RARα-treated cases.
source: Next, we monitored BMP activity (pSmad1/5/9), expression of Sox9 protein and foxd3 mRNA in embryos fixed at advanced stages of NC production prior to the normal downregulation of the above. The number of sections or segments with pSmad, Sox9, or foxd3 expression did not differ between control and VP16-RARα-treated cases (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D-N, see details in legend).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2D-N.

claim: The extent of neural crest emigration is reduced by 19% (p = 0.065, not significant) in VP16-RARα compared to control GFP-transfected neural tubes.
source: Next, the extent of NC emigration was reduced by 19% (p = 0.065, not significant) in VP16-RARα compared to control GFP-transfected NTs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Whereas RA signaling is necessary for the end of neural crest EMT and associated events, it is not sufficient to prematurely end these processes.
source: Together, whereas RA signaling is necessary for the end of NC EMT and associated events, it is not sufficient to prematurely end these processes.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data on gain of RA function.

claim: Expression of roof plate-specific BMP inhibitors is strongly reduced upon RA downregulation.
source: As described in Figure 2, expression of RP-specific BMP inhibitors was strongly reduced.
evidence: This claim refers to data shown in Figure 2.

claim: mRNA encoding Slit1 is decreased under experimental conditions of RA inhibition.
source: Likewise, mRNA encoding Slit1, a chemorepellent of post-floor plate commissural axons (Kidd et al., 1999) was also decreased under experimental conditions (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and a citation to previous work (Kidd et al., 1999).

claim: Additional roof plate markers, such as Rspo1, NDP (norrin), or draxin, are normally expressed upon RA inhibition.
source: In contrast, additional RP markers, such as Rspo1, NDP (norrin), or draxin, were normally expressed (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), suggesting that development of a number of RP traits is independent of RA signaling.
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Development of a number of roof plate traits is independent of RA signaling.
source: In contrast, additional RP markers, such as Rspo1, NDP (norrin), or draxin, were normally expressed (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), suggesting that development of a number of RP traits is independent of RA signaling.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data on roof plate marker expression.

claim: In control neural tubes, only Rspo1 is apparent in the roof plate, while in RARα403-treated embryos, both Rspo1 and foxd3 are detected in an overlapping pattern in the roof plate.
source: Whereas in control NTs, only Rspo1 was apparent in the RP, both Rspo1 and foxd3 were detected in an overlapping pattern in the RP of the treated embryos (Figure 6A–B''').
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 6A–B'''.

claim: SNAI2+Rspo1+ cells are present in the roof plate of RARα403-treated embryos.
source: In striking contrast, both markers were detected in the same dorsal NT cells in the absence of local RA signaling (Figure 6D–D", F–G", H1).
evidence: This claim is supported by combined immunostaining and fluorescent in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 6D–D".

claim: Sox9+Rspo1+ cells are present in the roof plate of RARα403-treated embryos.
source: In striking contrast, both markers were detected in the same dorsal NT cells in the absence of local RA signaling (Figure 6D–D", F–G", H1).
evidence: This claim is supported by combined immunostaining and fluorescent in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 6F–G".

claim: Rspo1+Sox9+ cells are noticed undergoing delamination from the neural tube in some instances.
source: In some instances, Rspo1+Sox9+ cells were also noticed undergoing delamination from the NT (Figure 6G–G", arrowhead).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6G–G".

claim: The onset of both BAMBI and Rspo1 mRNAs in the neural tube is similar in control and VP16-RARα-treated embryos.
source: Serial section analysis, performed in regions flanking the beginning of gene expression, revealed that the onset of both BAMBI and Rspo1 mRNAs in the NT was similar in control and VP16-RARα-treated embryos (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Loss of RA signaling does not totally prevent the advent of roof plate markers.
source: Together, these data show that the loss of RA signaling does not totally prevent the advent of RP markers and, reciprocally, high levels of RA signaling at the NC stage are not sufficient to promote a premature advent of RP-specific genes.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined experimental data on roof plate marker expression.

claim: High levels of RA signaling at the neural crest stage are not sufficient to promote a premature advent of roof plate-specific genes.
source: Together, these data show that the loss of RA signaling does not totally prevent the advent of RP markers and, reciprocally, high levels of RA signaling at the NC stage are not sufficient to promote a premature advent of RP-specific genes.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined experimental data on roof plate marker expression.

claim: Loss of neural crest identity and gain of roof plate fate are independently-regulated processes.
source: Hence, loss of NC identity and gain of RP fate are independently-regulated processes.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined experimental data.

claim: Timely RA activity in the dorsal neural tube is required for the proper segregation of neural crest from roof plate fates.
source: Nevertheless, timely RA activity in the dorsal NT is required for the proper segregation of NC from RP fates.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined experimental data.

claim: There is no significant difference in the number of BarHL1+ interneurons between control and RARα403-treated embryos.
source: Whereas no significant difference in the number of BarHL1+ interneurons could be monitored between control and treated embryos (Figure 7A), there was a collective dorsal shift in their position in the RARα403-treated NTs, with some of BarHL1+ cells residing in the RP domain itself (Figure 7B–E', arrowheads).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: There is a collective dorsal shift in the position of BarHL1+ interneurons in RARα403-treated neural tubes, with some cells residing in the roof plate domain itself.
source: Whereas no significant difference in the number of BarHL1+ interneurons could be monitored between control and treated embryos (Figure 7A), there was a collective dorsal shift in their position in the RARα403-treated NTs, with some of BarHL1+ cells residing in the RP domain itself (Figure 7B–E', arrowheads).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 7B–E'.

claim: The area of the Rspo1-positive roof plate does not significantly differ between control and RARα403-treated embryos.
source: This shift did not impact the overall size of the RP, as the area of the Rspo1-positive RP did not significantly differ between control and treated embryos (control, 1672 ± 121.3 μm2 (n = 8); compared to RARa403, 1790 ± 146.1 μm2 (n = 8), p = 0.544, student's t-test).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data.

claim: Inhibition of RA signaling does not affect roof plate-mediated formation of dI1 interneurons.
source: Thus, whereas inhibition of RA signaling does not affect RP-mediated formation of dI1 interneurons, it interferes with the spatial information conveyed onto dorsal interneurons from the RP, likely by impairing the formation of the boundary between the RP and more ventral domains.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data on dI1 interneuron development.

claim: Inhibition of RA signaling interferes with the spatial information conveyed onto dorsal interneurons from the roof plate, likely by impairing the formation of the boundary between the roof plate and more ventral domains.
source: Thus, whereas inhibition of RA signaling does not affect RP-mediated formation of dI1 interneurons, it interferes with the spatial information conveyed onto dorsal interneurons from the RP, likely by impairing the formation of the boundary between the RP and more ventral domains.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data on dI1 interneuron spatial distribution.

claim: RA signaling not necessarily influences development of roof plate properties but rather impairs temporal and spatial segregation between dorsal cell lineages.
source: These findings further indicate that RA signaling not necessarily influences development of RP properties but rather impairs temporal and spatial segregation between dorsal cell lineages.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined experimental data.

claim: RARα403 causes a mild 12% increase in the area of expression of Pax7 when compared to controls.
source: RARα403 caused a mild 12% increase in the area of expression of Pax7 when compared to controls (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-C), and had no effect on either the localization or extent of expression of Hb9 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D-F).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: RARα403 has no effect on either the localization or extent of expression of Hb9.
source: RARα403 caused a mild 12% increase in the area of expression of Pax7 when compared to controls (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-C), and had no effect on either the localization or extent of expression of Hb9 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D-F).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D-F.

claim: The effects of RA inhibition are directed to the dorsal neural tube and do not result from overall changes in its dorso-ventral patterning.
source: These data corroborate that the effects documented are directed to the dorsal NT and do not result from overall changes in its dorso-ventral patterning.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data on Pax7 and Hb9 expression.

claim: BAMBI remains strongly expressed in the roof plate of treated embryos to the same extent as the control sides, despite separation from the mesoderm.
source: Notably, BAMBI remained strongly expressed in the RP of treated embryos to the same extent as the control sides, despite separation from the mesoderm and virtual disappearance of the somitic tissue that lost contact with the NT (Figure 8A–C').
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 8A–C'.

claim: A comparable expression of BAMBI mRNA on both hemi-roof plates is apparent when the neural tube is split along the dorsal midline following insertion of a barrier between the neural tube and somites.
source: A comparable expression of BAMBI mRNA on both hemi-RPs was still apparent under these conditions (Figure 8E–F"), suggesting that the paraxial mesoderm is not the source of RA important for NC to RP transition.
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 8E–F".

claim: The paraxial mesoderm is not the source of RA important for neural crest to roof plate transition.
source: A comparable expression of BAMBI mRNA on both hemi-RPs was still apparent under these conditions (Figure 8E–F"), suggesting that the paraxial mesoderm is not the source of RA important for NC to RP transition.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data on mechanical separation of the mesoderm from the neural tube.

claim: Each of the factors foxd3, snai2, or sox9 cell-autonomously prevents the onset of Raldh2 expression in the roof plate.
source: Each of the factors cell-autonomously prevented the onset of Raldh2 expression in the RP when compared to control GFP-electroporated cases (Figure 9).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 9.

claim: Expression of neural crest (foxd3, snai2, sox9) and RA-associated roof plate traits (e.g; Raldh2) stand in a mutually repressive temporal relationship.
source: Hence, expression of NC (foxd3, snai2, sox9) and RA-associated RP traits (e.g; Raldh2) stand in a mutually repressive temporal relationship.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data on the interaction between neural crest genes and Raldh2.

claim: Dorsal neural tube-derived retinoic acid, via inhibition of BMP signaling, is an essential factor responsible for the end of neural crest generation and the proper segregation of dorsal neural lineages.
source: Collectively, our results demonstrate that neural tube-derived retinoic acid, via inhibition of BMP signaling, is an essential factor responsible for the end of neural crest generation and the proper segregation of dorsal neural lineages.
evidence: This claim summarizes the main findings of the study.
